content: Norethindrone is an oral contraceptive approved by the FDA for the prevention of pregnancy. Common side effects include nausea, headache, abnormal menstrual cycles, breast tenderness, and irregular periods. To achieve maximum contraceptive effectiveness, norethindrone tablets must be taken exactly as directed. One tablet should be taken every day at the same time, without any interruption between pill packs. The typical failure rate is estimated to be around 5%, often due to late or missed pills. There is limited information regarding off-label uses of norethindrone in both adult and pediatric patients. For pediatric patients, safety and efficacy have been established in postpubertal adolescents under the age of 16 and in users aged 16 years and older. However, its use before menarche is not indicated. Norethindrone is contraindicated in individuals with known or suspected pregnancy, breast carcinoma, undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, hypersensitivity to any component of the product, benign or malignant liver tumors, or acute liver disease. Cigarette smoking increases the risk of serious cardiovascular disease, and women using oral contraceptives should be strongly advised not to smoke. Norethindrone does not contain estrogen, and the risks associated with estrogen-containing combined oral contraceptives (COCs) are not discussed in this insert. The relationship between progestin-only oral contraceptives and these risks is not fully defined. Healthcare professionals should monitor for early symptoms of serious disease and discontinue oral contraceptive therapy when appropriate. The incidence of ectopic pregnancies among progestin-only oral contraceptive users is 5 per 1000 woman-years. Up to 10% of pregnancies reported in clinical studies of progestin-only oral contraceptive users are extrauterine. While a history of ectopic pregnancy is not a contraindication to this contraceptive method, healthcare professionals should remain vigilant for ectopic pregnancy in women who become pregnant or report lower abdominal pain while using progestin-only oral contraceptives. Delayed follicular atresia and ovarian cysts may occur, with follicles sometimes growing larger than in a normal cycle. These enlarged follicles generally resolve spontaneously and are often asymptomatic, though they may occasionally cause mild abdominal pain or, rarely, require surgical intervention if they twist or rupture. Irregular menstrual patterns are common among women using progestin-only oral contraceptives. If genital bleeding suggests infection, malignancy, or other abnormal conditions, nonpharmacologic causes should be ruled out. Prolonged amenorrhea should prompt evaluation for pregnancy. Some epidemiological studies have reported an increased relative risk of breast cancer among oral contraceptive users, particularly at younger ages and with longer durations of use. These studies predominantly involved combined oral contraceptives, and there is insufficient data to determine whether progestin-only pills (POPs) similarly increase the risk. Women with breast cancer should not use oral contraceptives due to the uncertain role of female hormones in breast cancer. Oral contraceptive use has been associated with an increased risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia in some populations, though the extent to which this is due to differences in sexual behavior and other factors remains controversial. There is insufficient data to determine whether POPs increase the risk of developing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. Benign hepatic adenomas have been associated with combined oral contraceptive use, though the incidence of benign tumors is rare in the United States. Rupture of benign hepatic adenomas may cause death through intra-abdominal hemorrhage. Studies have shown an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma in combined oral contraceptive users, but there is insufficient data to determine whether POPs increase the risk of hepatic neoplasia. Patients should be counseled that norethindrone does not protect against HIV infection (AIDS) or other sexually transmitted diseases. It is considered good medical practice for sexually active women using oral contraceptives to have annual history and physical examinations. Physical examinations may be deferred until after initiating oral contraceptives if deemed appropriate by the healthcare professional. Some users may experience slight deterioration in glucose tolerance, with increases in plasma insulin. Women with diabetes mellitus who use progestin-only oral contraceptives generally do not experience changes in their insulin requirements. However, prediabetic and diabetic women should be carefully monitored while taking POPs. Lipid metabolism may occasionally be affected, with decreases in HDL, HDL2, and apolipoprotein A-I and A-II, and increases in hepatic lipase. There is usually no effect on total cholesterol, HDL3, LDL, or VLDL. The onset or exacerbation of migraines or severe headaches with focal neurological symptoms requires discontinuation of progestin-only contraceptives and evaluation of the cause. Adverse reactions reported with the use of progestin-only pills include menstrual irregularity, frequent and irregular bleeding, headache, breast tenderness, nausea, dizziness, and, rarely, androgenic side effects such as acne, hirsutism, and weight gain. Other reported adverse reactions include fatigue, edema, vomiting, abdominal pain, hepatitis, jaundice, cholestatic pain, extremity pain, depression, nervousness, hypersensitivity reactions, alopecia, rash, pruritic rash, genital discharge, breast pain, delayed menstruation, suppressed lactation, vaginal hemorrhage, menorrhagia, and withdrawal bleeding upon discontinuation. The effectiveness of progestin-only pills may be reduced by hepatic enzyme-inducing drugs such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, and rifampin. Herbal products containing St. John’s Wort may also reduce contraceptive effectiveness and result in breakthrough bleeding. Concurrent use of bosentan and norethindrone-containing products may decrease hormone concentrations, increasing the risk of unintended pregnancy and unscheduled bleeding. Norethindrone is generally considered safe for use during breastfeeding, with no adverse effects on breastfeeding performance or infant health, growth, or development. However, isolated cases of decreased milk production have been reported. Small amounts of progestins pass into breast milk, resulting in detectable steroid levels in infant plasma. Norethindrone tablets are not indicated for use before menarche. Safety and efficacy are expected to be the same for postpubertal adolescents under 16 and users aged 16 years and older. There is no FDA guidance on the use of norethindrone in geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, or patients with renal or hepatic impairment. There is also no FDA guidance on its use in immunocompromised patients. Norethindrone is administered orally. Serum progestin levels peak approximately two hours after oral administration, followed by rapid distribution and elimination. By 24 hours after ingestion, serum levels return to near baseline, making efficacy dependent on strict adherence to the dosing schedule. There is significant variability in serum levels among individual users. Acute overdose of norethindrone has not been associated with serious adverse effects, including ingestion by children. There is limited information regarding chronic overdose. Norethindrone prevents conception by suppressing ovulation in approximately half of users, thickening cervical mucus to inhibit sperm penetration, lowering midcycle LH and FSH peaks, slowing ovum movement through the fallopian tubes, and altering the endometrium. Norethindrone is a white to creamy white, odorless crystalline powder that is stable in air. It is practically insoluble in water, soluble in chloroform and dioxane, sparingly soluble in alcohol, and slightly soluble in ether. Its chemical name is 17-Hydroxy-19-nor-17α-pregn-4-en-20-yn-3-one. Patients should be counseled on the importance of taking pills at the same time every day, using backup contraception if a pill is taken three or more hours late, and reporting prolonged bleeding, amenorrhea, or severe abdominal pain to their healthcare provider. They should also be advised to use barrier methods in addition to progestin-only oral contraceptives if at risk of contracting or transmitting STDs/HIV. Norethindrone should be stored at 20° to 25°C (68° to 77°F) and kept out of the reach of children.
